---
title: "Class 1 --- The U.S. health care paradox"
subtitle: "Thursday, August 27"
---

## What we covered

Course logistics, then the motivation. The U.S. spends more than anyone, leads on
medical innovation, and still does poorly on a lot of basic health outcomes. Most
of the class was about why those sit together, and why the usual one-line
explanations don't hold up. We also ran our first check-in and poll in Commons.

## Key points

- Life expectancy tracks how wealthy a country is. The U.S. takes the largest GDP
  gains in the G7 without the matching gain in life expectancy.
- Whether the system is good depends on who you are. With good insurance, near a
  hospital with the right capacity, it may be the best care in the world. Without
  that access, the same technology never gets deployed.
- Inefficiency and poor quality are different problems. You can be very
  inefficient and still deliver very good care.
- Maternal and infant mortality are where we look worst, partly because of who
  they happen to. Births are concentrated among lower-income households, Medicaid
  is the largest payer for births, and access there is most limited.
- The common explanations don't carry much weight.
    - *Less healthy.* More obesity and cardiovascular disease, but far less
      smoking and drinking. Doesn't explain the spending.
    - *Overuse.* Japan uses far more imaging than we do. We aren't the heaviest
      user of everything.
    - *Physician pay.* High, but the margin over other high-paying work here looks
      like the margin in other developed countries.
    - *Fraud.* Real, and visible right now in Medicare Advantage settlements, but
      small as a share of spending.
    - *Administrative waste.* Real and large. Every provider deals at once with
      many payers running different rules.
- Prices are the main answer. Same procedure, far more money here.
- Six things make health care interesting to an economist, and they're all present
  at once. Heterogeneous products, asymmetric information between patient and
  physician, unobservable quality, unpredictable need, insurance killing the
  incentive to shop, and adverse selection.
- Health care isn't even an experience good, since you often can't judge quality
  after consuming it. In the induction example, everyone comes out fine, the
  mother reasonably calls it the best care she's ever had, and she has no way to
  know whether earlier decisions were bad ones.
- With adverse selection, the cost of insurance depends on who buys it. The
  airline club and the all-you-can-eat buffet are the same problem.

## Clarifications and corrections

- **Medicaid share of births.** I said almost half. It's closer to 40 percent,
  40.2 percent in 2024 and 41.5 percent in 2023 (CDC/NCHS). Still the largest
  single payer for births. It runs from roughly 30 percent in some states to over
  60 percent in Louisiana, and above 75 percent for mothers under 20.
- **Elective induction.** I said it raises the chance of needing a cesarean. That
  was the older observational reading, since overturned. The ARRIVE trial
  (Grobman et al., *NEJM* 2018) found a lower cesarean rate with elective
  induction at 39 weeks. The example still works, but take the direction out of
  your notes.
- **"It's the prices, stupid."** I credited Uwe Reinhardt. The article is
  Anderson, Reinhardt, Hussey, and Petrosyan, *Health Affairs* (2003). Reinhardt
  is a coauthor.
- **Defensive medicine across countries.** Asked in class, and I still don't have
  an answer. The legal systems differ too much for a clean comparison.
  Domestically, many states adopted tort reform over thirty years and the
  estimated effects on spending have been small. It should have been on the
  common-explanations slide, and I'll add it.
